nameStory: The Master's Dart gets its name from the dart-like markings on its forewings that resemble arrowheads or spear points. The "Master's" part honors early moth collectors who admired this species' particularly well-defined dart markings compared to other cutworm moths.
description: Master's Dart is a medium-sized brown moth that's part of the cutworm moth family, so named because their caterpillars often "cut" plant stems at ground level. Adults have a wingspan of about 1.3 to 1.7 inches across, with mottled brown and gray wings that help them blend perfectly with tree bark during the day. Like most cutworm moths, they're nocturnal and are often attracted to porch lights and outdoor lamps on summer and fall evenings.

idTips.label: Dart-shaped wing markings
idTips.description: Look for distinctive arrow-point or dart-shaped markings on the brown forewings that give this moth its name - these appear as darker outlined shapes against the mottled background

idTips.label: Mottled brown coloration
idTips.description: Wings have a complex pattern of browns, grays, and subtle lighter patches that feels rough and bark-like when viewed up close

idTips.label: Medium wingspan
idTips.description: Measures 34-44mm across when wings are spread - roughly the size of a large postage stamp or small cookie

idTips.label: Nocturnal behavior
idTips.description: Active at night and drawn to artificial lights, often found resting motionless on tree trunks or walls during daylight hours

idTips.label: Robust moth body
idTips.description: Has a thick, fuzzy body typical of cutworm moths that feels substantial if gently handled - not delicate like many other moth families

habitat: Master's Dart moths can be found throughout New England in diverse habitats including suburban gardens, agricultural areas, forest edges, and open woodlands. They're particularly common around areas with mixed vegetation since their caterpillars feed on such a wide variety of plants. You'll often spot adults near outdoor lights in both rural and urban settings.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active during spring months. This is when overwintering caterpillars may be finishing their development underground.
seasonality.summer: Adults begin emerging in July and can be found at outdoor lights on warm evenings. Peak activity often occurs in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through October, making this an excellent time to spot them at porch lights and in gardens. This is their main flight season.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity during winter months. The species overwinters as caterpillars or pupae in the soil.

funFact: Master's Dart caterpillars are natural "night shift workers" - they hide underground during the day and emerge after dark to munch on plants, which is why gardeners often find mysteriously severed seedlings in the morning with no sign of the culprit!
confusionNotes: Master's Dart is easily confused with its close relative, the Dingy Cutworm Moth, which is similar in size and brown coloration. The key difference is in the wing markings - Master's Dart has those distinctive sharp dart or arrow-point shapes on the forewings, while Dingy Cutworm Moth has more subdued, less defined markings.
contextualKnowledge: The term "cutworm" refers to the larval stage of these moths, not the adults themselves. Many gardeners know cutworms as destructive pests that cut down young plants, but they may not realize these caterpillars transform into the brown moths they see at their porch lights.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Dingy Cutworm Moth, Master's Dart has much more pronounced and clearly defined dart-shaped markings on its forewings. While both species are mottled brown and similar in size, Master's Dart's wing patterns are generally more contrasted and easier to make out. Both are attracted to lights and active during the same late summer and fall period.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the Master's Dart, the dingy cutworm moth typically appears more uniformly brown and less contrasted in its wing markings.
